propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision confirming RPD refusal of refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dated October 20, 2021 confirming the refusal of their refugee claim by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).

propositions.text: RPD and RAD concluded Applicants have viable internal flight alternatives in Delhi and Mumbai, so not refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD and the RAD concluded that the Applicants have viable internal flight alternatives (IFAs) in Delhi and Mumbai and, accordingly, are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision confirming RPD refusal; RPD and RAD found viable internal flight alternatives in Delhi and Mumbai.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application for judicial review is dismissed.

propositions.text: RAD assessed evidence and submissions against accepted test for viable IFA.
propositions.quote: The RAD assessed the Applicants’ evidence and submissions against the accepted test for a viable IFA.

propositions.text: RAD justified conclusions on motivation and means of Applicants’ agents of persecution with detailed reasons responding to Vavilov framework.
propositions.quote: The RAD also justified its conclusions regarding the motivation and means of the Applicants’ agents of persecution to pursue them in the IFAs with detailed reasons that respond to the review framework established in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 (Vavilov).

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review, finds RAD properly assessed evidence and justified conclusions per Vavilov framework.

propositions.text: Applicants are Indian citizens; Principal Applicant owned garment factory in Jalandhar, Punjab.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of India. Prior to coming to Canada, Paramjit Singh (the Principal Applicant) owned and ran a garment factory in Jalandhar (Punjab), India.

propositions.text: In 2018, Principal Applicant borrowed money from financier BS but factory fire prevented repayment; BS and henchmen attacked him and damaged property.
propositions.quote: In 2018, he borrowed money from a loan financier, BS, but later the same year suffered a catastrophic fire at the factory. As a result, when BS demanded repayment of the loan, the Principal Applicant was unable to make the required payment. On September 20, 2018, BS and his henchmen went to the Applicants’ home, beat the Principal Applicant and destroyed property.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicants are Indian citizens; Principal Applicant owned factory, borrowed money, suffered fire, then was attacked by financier BS and henchmen.

propositions.text: On October 15, 2018, Punjab police detained Principal Applicant on theft allegations by competitor HS and for militant involvement; detained three days.
propositions.quote: On October 15, 2018, the local Punjab police detained the Principal Applicant based on allegations of theft by one of his business competitors, HS. The police also accused the Principal Applicant of being involved with militants and detained him for three days.

propositions.text: On November 5, 2018, Principal Applicant went into hiding in New Delhi; family joined November 12, 2018.
propositions.quote: On November 5, 2018, the Principal Applicant went into hiding in New Delhi where his family joined him on November 12, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Principal Applicant detained by Punjab police on theft and militant allegations, then went into hiding in New Delhi with family.

propositions.text: With agent's help, Principal Applicant, spouse, and one son obtained Canadian visas and left India October 29, 2019; one son remained in India.
propositions.quote: With the assistance of an agent, the Principal Applicant, his spouse and one of their sons obtained Canadian visas and left India on October 29, 2019. One of the couple’s sons remained in India.

propositions.text: Applicants claimed refugee protection November 8, 2019, fearing persecution by Punjab police, competitor HS, and financier BS if returned.
propositions.quote: The Applicants claimed refugee protection on November 8, 2019, stating that, should they be forced to return to India, they fear persecution by the police in Punjab, the competitor HS, and unpaid loan financier BS.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Applicants left India with visas in 2019, claimed refugee protection fearing persecution by police, competitor HS, and financier BS.

propositions.text: RPD rejected refugee claims May 3, 2021, finding two internal flight alternatives available; Applicants appealed to RAD.
propositions.quote: Following a hearing on May 3, 2021, the RPD rejected the Applicants’ refugee claims on the basis that there are two IFAs available to them within India. The Applicants appealed the RPD’s decision to the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Court states RPD rejected refugee claims due to available IFAs; Applicants appealed to RAD.

propositions.text: RAD agreed with RPD that Applicants failed to prove agents of persecution motivated or able to locate them in Delhi or Mumbai, or that relocation unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Following an analysis of the Applicants’ appeal arguments, the RAD agreed with the RPD that the Applicants had not established that their agents of persecution are motivated or able to locate them in Delhi or Mumbai, or that it would be unreasonable in the circumstances for them to seek refuge in the IFAs.

propositions.text: Applicants challenged RPD findings on both prongs of viable IFA test from Rasaratnam.
propositions.quote: On appeal to the RAD, the Applicants challenged the RPD’s findings on both prongs of the established test for a viable IFA set out in Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 FC 706 (CA) (Rasaratnam).

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found Applicants failed to prove agents motivated or able to find them in IFAs; Applicants challenged both prongs of IFA test.

propositions.text: RAD found police and HS lack continuing motivation to locate Applicants as Principal Applicant won't compete with HS if relocated.
propositions.quote: Neither the police nor HS have a continuing motivation to locate the Applicants as the Principal Applicant will no longer compete with HS if he relocates to either of the IFAs.

propositions.text: Police interest stemmed from HS's competitive jealousy; no evidence police approached son living near Jalandhar, undermining police motivation claim.
propositions.quote: The police would therefore have no interest in the Applicants because their alleged pursuit stemmed from HS and his competitive jealousy. There was no evidence before the RPD or the RAD that the police have approached the Principal Applicant’s son who continues to reside in Punjab, only 60 kilometres from Jalandhar. The lack of police pursuit of the son undermines the Applicants’ contention that the police remain motivated to seek them throughout India.

propositions.text: Credibility concerns with Applicants' police visit allegations to local Councillor and brother-in-law's home; omissions in BOC unexplained.
propositions.quote: There are credibility concerns with the Applicants’ allegation of police visits to their local Councillor. These visits were not mentioned in their Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative or in any amendment to the BOC. The Principal Applicant’s explanation that it is normal for the police to “go around in order to look for someone” is not a reasonable explanation for the omission. There are also credibility concerns with the Applicants’ allegation that the police searched for the Principal Applicant at his brother-in-law’s home in Delhi.

propositions.text: Applicants failed to establish Punjab police have means to locate them in Delhi or Mumbai; no official police interest evidence like charges, warrants, or FIRs.
propositions.quote: The Applicants have not established that the Punjab police have the means to locate them in Delhi or Mumbai. First, there is no documentary evidence of official police interest in the Principal Applicant, such as actual charges against him, an arrest warrant, a First Information Report (FIR), or other evidence suggesting the Principal Applicant may have been entered in a crime and criminal tracking network or database.

propositions.text: NDP shows police stations in India poorly connected with ineffective data sharing; tracking individuals usually only for heinous crimes.
propositions.quote: Second, there is information in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for India that police stations across India are not well connected, nor is there a system of effective data storage and sharing. Police in India are able to track persons of interest when they put their minds to it but the effort to track an individual is typically made only in cases involving heinous crimes (e.g., rape, murder).

propositions.text: RAD acknowledged police could alert Punjab police to Applicants' whereabouts but Applicants failed to prove they would not be safe in IFAs.
propositions.quote: The RAD acknowledged that problems with the police can arise in the absence of a formal arrest warrant or accusation and that the police in the IFAs could alert the Punjab police to the Applicants’ whereabouts. However, the Applicants’ assertion to this effect did not discharge their onus of establishing they would not be safe in the IFAs.

propositions.text: RAD discounted Applicants' reliance on tenant verification system for police tracking.
propositions.quote: The RAD discounted the Applicants’ reliance on the ability of the police to find them through the tenant verification system.

propositions.text: Regarding BS, Principal Applicant knew little; no evidence BS sought them since 2018 or could locate them in IFAs; wealth or business outside Punjab insufficient.
propositions.quote: Turning to BS, the Principal Applicant knew little about this individual except that he is a financier. The Applicants provided no evidence that BS had sought them since 2018 or of how he could locate them in the IFAs. The Applicants’ allegation that BS is wealthy or may possibly have business outside of Punjab was not sufficient to est

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found police and HS lack motivation to locate Applicants; credibility concerns on police visit claims; no evidence police have means to find them; BS unlikely to locate them.

propositions.text: RAD's reasons and conclusions on IFAs are reviewed for reasonableness per Vavilov and Sadiq.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s reasons and conclusions regarding the availability of IFAs in India for the Applicants are subject to review for reasonableness (Vavilov at paras 10, 23; Sadiq v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 430 at para 32).

propositions.text: Reasonableness review examines if decision is internally coherent, rational, and justified by facts and law (Vavilov para 85).
propositions.quote: Where the Court reviews an administrative decision for reasonableness, its role is to examine the reasons given by the decision maker and determine whether the decision “is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: Court states RAD's IFA decision reviewed for reasonableness per Vavilov, requiring coherent, rational, justified analysis.

propositions.text: IFA concept integral to Convention refugee definition; claimant must be refugee from country, not region.
propositions.quote: The concept of an IFA is integral to the definition of a Convention refugee. A claimant must be a refugee from a country, not from a particular region of a country.

propositions.text: IFA test has two prongs: serious possibility of persecution or section 97 risk in IFA, and reasonableness of relocation (Rasaratnam para 13).
propositions.quote: The IFA test has two prongs: is there a serious possibility of persecution or a section 97 risk in the proposed IFA, and is it reasonable for the claimant(s) to relocate there? (Rasaratnam at para 13).

propositions.text: Once IFA issue raised, claimant bears onus to prove no viable IFA (Thirunavukkarasu).
propositions.quote: Once the issue of an IFA has been raised, the claimant bears the onus of establishing that they do not have a viable IFA (Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589, at p 594-595 (CA)).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains IFA test and claimant's onus to prove no viable IFA once issue raised.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD's analysis of police motivation and means to locate them in IFAs is unreasonable and selectively reads NDP evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the RAD’s analysis of both the motivation and means of the police in India to locate them in the IFAs is unreasonable and reflects a selective reading of the documentary evidence in the NDP.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD's analysis of police motivation and means is unreasonable and selectively reads evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants acknowledge police interest cause ended but argue police still look in old neighbourhood and did visit brother-in-law's Delhi home in 2018; RAD erred in stating otherwise.
propositions.quote: In the course of their submissions regarding the ongoing motivation of the police, the Applicants acknowledge that the underlying cause for police interest in them no longer exists. However, the Applicants argue that the police in Punjab continue to look for them in their old neighbourhood and that the RAD erred in stating that the police have not attempted to locate them in Delhi. They state that the police did, in fact, visit the Delhi home of the Principal Applicant’s brother-in-law in 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue police still look for them in old area and visited brother-in-law's home; RAD erred in denying this.

propositions.text: Court not persuaded by Applicants' argument; finds no material error in RAD's assessment of police interest.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by the Applicants’ argument and find no material error in the RAD’s assessment of the continued interest of the Punjab and Delhi police to locate the Principal Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicants' argument and finds no material error in RAD's assessment of police interest.

propositions.text: RAD noted Principal Applicant testified police visited brother-in-law's home Nov 10, 2018 but no mention in BOC; brother-in-law affidavit referenced police visit to Applicants' home but not his own.
propositions.quote: The RAD referred to the Principal Applicant’s testimony at the RPD hearing that the police had gone to his brother-in-law’s home in Delhi on November 10, 2018 but stated that there is no reference in his BOC narrative to such police visits. The panel noted that the brother‑in-law’s affidavit referenced the police visit to the Applicants’ home on November 10, 2018 but did not mention police visits to his own home.

propositions.text: RAD found credibility concerns with police search allegation at brother-in-law's home; even if visit occurred, police did not return, indicating lack of interest.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I find there are credibility concerns with the allegation that the police searched for the [Principal Applicant] at the brother-in-law’s home in Delhi. Nevertheless, even if I assume the police did attend at the brother-in-law’s house on November 10, 2018, the Appellants testified that the police did not return thereafter. I find this further signals a lack of interest by the police in the Appellants and renders it unlikely that they would go to the lengths of seeking them in an IFA, including in Delhi.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found no BOC mention of police visit to brother-in-law's home; credibility concerns; even if visit occurred, police did not return, showing lack of interest.

propositions.text: Brother-in-law affidavit states police visited Applicants' home Nov 10, 2018 and came to their house looking for Principal Applicant who had left.
propositions.quote: In his affidavit, the brother-in-law stated that the Principal Applicant came to his house on November 5, 2018 and informed him that the police had visited the Applicants’ home in Jalandhar five days earlier, on November 10, 2018. The brother-in-law also stated, “[t]hat the police came to our house looking for him but he was already gone”.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant confirmed police went to brother-in-law's home in Delhi Nov 10, 2018 but he had left; police did not return.
propositions.quote: Before the RPD, the Principal Applicant confirmed that the police went to his brother-in-law’s home in Delhi but that he had already left to stay elsewhere. The Principal Applicant also testified that the police visit in Delhi was on November 10, 2018 and that the police did not subsequently return to the brother‑in-law’s home.

paragraphs.summary: Brother-in-law affidavit and Principal Applicant confirm police visited brother-in-law's home Nov 10, 2018 but did not return.

propositions.text: Court agrees RAD erred in stating brother-in-law omitted police visit mention but finds error insignificant and not undermining conclusion of no police interest since Nov 2018.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicants that the RAD erred in stating that the brother-in-law omitted from his affidavit any mention of a police visit to his own home. However, I find that the error is not a significant error and does not undermine the RAD’s substantive conclusion that the police have demonstrated no interest in pursuing the Applicants since November 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's error about brother-in-law affidavit insignificant and not undermining conclusion of no police interest since 2018.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant left brother-in-law's home shortly after wife and sons arrived Nov 12, 2018; agent kept family in hiding until departure.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant left the brother-in-law’s home shortly after his wife and two sons arrived in Delhi on November 12, 2018. In his BOC, the Principal Applicant states that he met with the agent who assisted the family in obtaining visas on November 12 and that the agent kept the family in hiding following the meeting until their departure from India.

propositions.text: Chronology supports police visit to brother-in-law's home occurred shortly after Nov 12, 2018.
propositions.quote: Although it is not possible to determine the exact date of the police visit to the brother-in-law’s home in Delhi, the Principal Applicant’s testimony, the chronology of events in November 2018 and the brother-in-law’s affidavit support the conclusion that the visit occurred shortly after November 12, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds chronology supports police visit to brother-in-law's home shortly after Nov 12, 2018; Principal Applicant left home then and was kept in hiding.

propositions.text: Applicants do not contest police interest caused by HS's jealousy would end upon relocation; do not contest RAD's findings on omissions in BOC.
propositions.quote: The Applicants do not contest the fact that police interest in the Principal Applicant was spurred by HS and that his competitive jealousy would no longer exist upon their relocation. They do not contest the RAD’s conclusions regarding omissions from the Principal Applicant’s BOC relating to police visits to the municipal councillor in Punjab, their adult son who lives close to their hometown or their neighbours in Punjab.

propositions.text: RAD assumed police visit to brother-in-law's home occurred; three-year gap since police interest undermines continuing motivation claim.
propositions.quote: Despite its statement that the evidence did not support the fact of a police visit in Delhi, the RAD was prepared to assume that a visit occurred on November 10, 2018. Whether the visit occurred on November 10, 2018 or a few days later once the Principal Applicant had left his brother-in-law’s home, the evidence in the record supports the panel’s conclusion that the three-year interval since the Delhi police displayed any interest in the Principal Applicant undermines the allegation of continuing police motivation.

propositions.text: RAD's factual error about brother-in-law affidavit does not affect conclusion; Principal Applicant's general affidavit reference to police visits omitted from BOC also does not affect conclusion.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s factual error regarding the brother-in-law’s affidavit does not affect this conclusion, nor does the Principal Applicant’s general reference in his affidavit (omitted from his BOC) to police visits to his neighbours in Punjab.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicants do not contest police interest cause ending; RAD's assumption of police visit and three-year gap undermine continuing motivation; factual error insignificant.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD selectively read NDP, unreasonably relied on police disorganization and absence of warrant or FIR, ignoring arrest and fingerprinting.
propositions.quote: Turning to the RAD’s analysis of the means of the police in India to locate them in the IFAs, the Applicants submit that the panel’s reasoning reflects a selective reading of the NDP. They argue that the RAD unreasonably relied on excerpts from the NDP that speak to the lack of organization among police forces in India and over-emphasized the absence of a warrant or FIR against the Principal Applicant. They state that the RAD failed to recognize the fact that the Principal Applicant was arrested, his fingerprints taken and reporting conditions imposed on him by the police in Punjab.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD selectively read NDP and overemphasized lack of warrant or FIR, ignoring arrest and fingerprinting.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Applicants; RAD's nuanced analysis acknowledges police may act without warrant but usually only for heinous crimes; jealousy-based accusations not heinous.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the Applicants’ submissions for two reasons. First, the RAD’s analysis of the ability of the police to track the Principal Applicant in the absence of a warrant or FIR is nuanced. The RAD acknowledges the possibility that police forces may act in the absence of formal documentation but notes that action is typically taken only in the face of heinous crimes or crimes of significant notoriety. I am not persuaded by the Applicants’ statement that the accusations against the Principal Applicant prompted by a jealous competitor fall within those parameters.

propositions.text: Court finds no error in RAD's statement that absence of warrant or FIR makes it unlikely Principal Applicant is in national criminal database.
propositions.quote: I find no error in the RAD’s statement that the absence of any official police interest in the Principal Applicant in the form of a warrant or FIR make it unlikely that he would be entered into a nationally accessible criminal database.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicants' argument, finds RAD's nuanced analysis reasonable; jealousy-based accusations not heinous; no error in finding no warrant or FIR likely means no national database entry.

propositions.text: Applicants' insistence on possible extra-judicial police problems is speculative and does not meet their burden of proof.
propositions.quote: I also agree with the RAD that the Applicants’ insistence on the possibility of problems with the police occurring extra-judicially is speculative and does not discharge their onus of establishing they would not be safe in the IFAs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicants' claim about extra-judicial police problems speculative and insufficient to meet their burden.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded the RAD failed to address critical contradictory documentation in the NDP.
propositions.quote: Second and more generally, I am not persuaded that the RAD failed to address critical and contradictory documentation in the NDP (Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] FCJ No 1425).

propositions.text: Applicants argue NDP shows not all police stations in India are disorganized or slow and police can use CCTNS and tenant verification systems.
propositions.quote: The Applicants include in their written submissions information from the NDP stating that not all police stations in all states in India are disorganized or slow to respond and that the police can use the CCTNS, the pan-India database on crime and criminals, and the tenant verification system to access the criminal record and history of a person from any police station in the country.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Applicants' argument that the RAD failed to address contradictory NDP documentation about police organization and databases.

propositions.text: Excerpts cited by Applicants do not contradict RAD's assessment of NDP or Applicants' claims.
propositions.quote: The excerpts cited by the Applicants provide information regarding the organization and ability of certain police forces to take action but does not contradict the RAD’s assessment of the NDP or the specific facts and circumstances of the Applicants’ claims.

propositions.text: Recent evidence shows significant shortcomings in pan-India registration systems; RAD's analysis is thorough.
propositions.quote: The recent documentary evidence establishes significant shortcomings in the various pan-India registration systems and the RAD’s analysis of the operational status of the criminal and tenant registration systems in India is thorough.

propositions.text: RAD noted inadequate tenant system in Delhi and Mumbai and police resource shortages for verifications.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s decision includes reference to the inadequate state of the latter system in Delhi and Mumbai, and to the lack of resources of many police forces to carry out verifications.

propositions.text: Applicants cite 2018 Times of India statement that CCTNS was used and most police stations integrated into system.
propositions.quote: The Applicants refer to a statement from the Times of India newspaper in 2018 that the CCTNS was being used and that the vast majority of police stations in India were integrated into the system.

propositions.text: Statements describe intended scope of systems but do not address gaps in implementation and usage.
propositions.quote: However, that statement and the passages from the NDP included in the Applicants’ written submissions set out the intended scope and operation of those systems but do not address the clear gaps in implementation and actual usage.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicants' cited evidence does not contradict RAD's thorough analysis of police registration system shortcomings.

propositions.text: Applicants' reliance on NDP to assert police tracking possibility lacks evidence and does not show RAD error.
propositions.quote: I find that the Applicants’ reliance on portions of the NDP to assert the possibility the Principal Applicant would be tracked to either of the IFAs, without evidence of why the police would do so, does not establish a reviewable error in the RAD’s analysis of the means of the police to locate them in the IFAs.

propositions.text: No evidence Principal Applicant's name is in CCTNS; allegations make police unlikely to devote resources to locate him.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence in the record that the Principal Applicant’s name has been included in the CCTNS and, as the RAD stated, the allegations against the Principal Applicant are such that it is unlikely the police forces would devote scarce resources to locating him in the IFAs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence supports Applicants' claim police would track Principal Applicant; no RAD error found.

propositions.text: RAD's finding of viable IFAs is reasonable and its analysis clear and comprehensive; application dismissed.
propositions.quote: In summary, the RAD’s finding of viable IFAs for the Applicants in India is reasonable in light of the evidence and applicable law, and its analysis is clear and comprehensive. As a result, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes RAD's decision is reasonable and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: No question for certification proposed or arises; judicial review application dismissed.
propositions.quote: No question for certification was proposed by the parties and none arises in this case. JUDGMENT IN IMM-8223-21 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review and certifies no question of general importance.
